parrafos: Much of the area around Gettysburg still looks like it did in the 1860s, during the American Civil War. The town is in the middle of good farmland. Roads pass through Gettysburg that lead to Baltimore, Washington, D.C., and other eastern cities. It is hard to believe that two huge armies fought there.

One fighting force was the United States Army of the Potomac, commanded by General George Meade. The other was the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia led by General Robert E. Lee. Lee’s troops had moved north into Pennsylvania from Virginia.
Lee believed that a Southern win of a battle on Northern land would force a negotiated settlement of the Civil War and mean independence for the Confederate States.
The battle of Gettysburg began on July 1, 1863. About 170,000 soldiers fought for three days. When it ended on July 3, more than 50,000 soldiers were dead, wounded or missing.

Many visitors start their visit to Gettysburg at the Gettysburg Museum of the Civil War. The museum has a large collection of Civil War objects. The museum has more than 1 million artifacts, from soldiers’ private notebooks and clothing to maps of the battlefield.

The painting shows the artist’s vision of the final major attack of the battle on July 3, 1863. Over time, it has come to be called Pickett's Charge. George Pickett was one of several Confederate commanders ordered to make the charge.
The Confederate soldiers reached a point close to the northern lines and headquarters. Today, the point is called the “High Water Mark.” Northern forces then turned the Confederates back.

The charge failed. Southern forces would never again reach so far north. Soon after the battle, people began to visit Gettysburg to try to understand what happened there. One of those visitors, on November 19, 1863, was President Abraham Lincoln. He was invited to help dedicate a burial ground for Union soldiers killed in the battle.
Nancy Steinbach and Ashley Thompson with additional material from the National Park Service for VOA Learning English. Mario Ritter, Jr. adapted it for the VOA Learning English podcast.
resumen_es: Presentación de Gettysburg, escenario en 1863 de una de las batallas decisivas de la guerra de Secesión, de su museo y de la carga de Pickett, que marcó el punto máximo del avance confederado.

ideas_clave.idea: The countryside around Gettysburg has hardly changed since the 1860s, which makes it difficult to imagine that a massive battle took place there.
The battle opposed Meade's Union army and Lee's Confederate army, which had invaded the North hoping that a victory there would force peace talks and Southern independence.
Some 170,000 men fought for three days in July 1863, and over 50,000 ended up dead, wounded or missing.
Visitors often begin at the Civil War museum, with over a million objects and a painting of the last great Confederate assault, known as Pickett's Charge.
The Confederates came close to the Union lines at the so-called High Water Mark but were repelled, and the South never again advanced so far north.
The site soon attracted visitors, including President Lincoln, who came in November 1863 to dedicate a cemetery for Union soldiers; the piece was written for VOA Learning English.

resumen_modelo: The text describes Gettysburg, a Pennsylvania farming town that still looks much as it did in the 1860s. In July 1863 it witnessed a decisive Civil War battle in which General Lee's Confederate army, hoping that a victory in the North would secure Southern independence, faced General Meade's Union forces. After three days of fighting, over 50,000 men were dead, wounded or missing. Today a museum recalls Pickett's Charge, the final Confederate assault, which failed after reaching the so-called High Water Mark. A few months later, President Lincoln came to dedicate a cemetery for the Union dead.

preguntas.pregunta: Who commanded the United States Army of the Potomac?
preguntas.cita: One fighting force was the United States Army of the Potomac, commanded by General George Meade.
preguntas.explicacion: Meade mandaba el ejército de la Unión. Lee dirigía el ejército confederado, Pickett era uno de sus comandantes y Lincoln era el presidente, no el jefe militar en la batalla.

preguntas.pregunta: Why did General Lee decide to fight in the North?
respuestas: He thought that defeating the Union on its own territory would oblige the North to negotiate an end to the war and accept the independence of the Confederate States.
preguntas.cita: Lee believed that a Southern win of a battle on Northern land would force a negotiated settlement of the Civil War
preguntas.explicacion: La respuesta debe explicar el objetivo estratégico: una victoria en territorio del Norte forzaría una paz negociada y la independencia del Sur.

preguntas.explicacion: «Negotiated settlement» es un acuerdo o arreglo negociado; «settlement» también significa «asentamiento» en otros contextos.

preguntas.cita: About 170,000 soldiers fought for three days.

preguntas.explicacion: El cuadro representa el último gran ataque, la carga de Pickett. No muestra el primer día, la visita de Lincoln ni la retirada de Lee.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the 'High Water Mark' and why is it significant?
respuestas: It is the point near the Union lines and headquarters that the Confederate soldiers reached during Pickett's Charge. It is significant because it was the furthest the Southern forces ever got: they were pushed back and never advanced so far north again.
preguntas.cita: Today, the point is called the “High Water Mark.” Northern forces then turned the Confederates back.
preguntas.explicacion: Hay que explicar qué es (el punto más avanzado del ataque) y su valor simbólico (el máximo avance confederado, seguido del fracaso definitivo).

glosario.nota: En la guerra de Secesión, «Union» designa al Norte y «Confederacy» al Sur.
Se usa para heridas de guerra o con arma; «injured» para accidentes.
Falso amigo parcial: no equivale a «artefactos» (dispositivos).
En empresas: sede central. Siempre con -s.
Aquí no es «dedicar» sino inaugurar solemnemente.
